newsitem.title: USA: Full UPS strike impact unknown for months - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Full UPS strike impact unknown for months - analysts.

text.p: United Parcel Service was expected to return to full operations on Wednesday, but analysts said it would be months before management would know the full impact of a crippling strike by 185,000 Teamster employees.

A day after the world's largest package delivery company struck a tentative deal with the union, Chief Executive James Kelly said UPS would move quickly to mobilize its ground and air delivery operations at more than 1,700 U.S. facilities.

"The strike tomorrow will be ancient history," Kelly told a news conference at UPS headquarters in Atlanta on Tuesday. "We have some limited operations today and we expect to have a full, total operation tomorrow."
Kelly said the proposed five-year contract with the Teamsters was financially acceptable and would allow UPS to remain competitive.

But company managers warned that UPS would have to lay off some strikers, perhaps as many as 15,500, because of business lost to rival delivery companies and the U.S. Postal Service during the 15-day work stoppage.
"The reality is that (the Teamsters are) not all coming back, and there will be fewer jobs," Kelly said.
"The strike doesn't help anyone. It's hurt us, it's hurt our employees and it's hurt our customers, and we've lost business. We've had customers tell us they will not be back."

UPS, with $22.4 billion in annual sales, had handed 80 percent of package deliveries in the United States before the strike, 12 million parcels sent to business offices, manufacturers, hospitals and consumers each day.
But the nation's biggest strike in two decades held operations at UPS to less than 10 percent of normal.

That saddled UPS with an overall loss of more than $650 million and raised fears that as much as 5 percent of the company's business had left for good as customers scrambled to find more secure avenues for moving vital shipments.

Promising it would not raise shipping rates to compensate for strike losses, UPS planned to begin phoning 1.6 million customers to assure them that service was returning to normal. The company also expected to make hundreds of thousands of "personal" visits to larger customers.
As much as 40 percent of the company's business was believed to have migrated into the hands of other shippers during the walkout.

But transportation industry analysts expected most UPS customers -- particularly small businesses -- to return, simply because rivals including Federal Express Corp. had not been able to cope with the volume of parcels left undelivered.
Standard & Poor's Corp. analyst Bob Schulz said UPS would probably have to wait six months before it could gauge the strike's final cost.

"There's no way they can get back every customer they had before the strike," he said. "In the short-term, most of the volume's going to return. But clearly, there will be people on the margins who start using two providers instead of one."

Analysts said the long-term effects of the strike also would depend on the new contract's toll on UPS' total costs. With only preliminary details available, however, that assessment also would have to wait.

The pact would create 10,000 new full-time jobs from an existing pool of part-time workers, who account for about two-thirds of the company's 301,000 employees in the United States. It also would raise average hourly wages for part-time workers from $11 to $15 over the life of the contract.

Kelly admitted that the company's biggest concession to the Teamsters had been on pensions. UPS abandoned a proposal to withdraw from a union-run multi-employer pension fund and set up a separate plan solely for UPS employees.

"Negotiation is a series of compromises, and there were dozens and dozens of issues that were compromised on. Unfortunately, the pension issue got the most press and that was the one where we compromised the most," he said.
